claims.text: Reduced grain size is the dominant factor governing wear resistance in HEA protective coatings.
Increasing grain-boundary density and efficacy enhances strain accommodation during frictional contact.
Enhanced strain accommodation mitigates severe plastic deformation during frictional contact.
As-deposited HEA coatings typically have ultrafine to nanocrystalline grain sizes.
Controlled thermal annealing can systematically refine or coarsen the coating grain size while preserving overall chemical composition.
Finer grains produce a higher density of grain boundaries.
A higher density of grain boundaries distributes local strain more uniformly during wear.
More uniform strain accommodation reduces localized deformation.
Reduced localized deformation delays microcrack formation.
Reduced localized deformation delays wear-particle delamination.
HEA coatings with smaller grains will have lower wear rates than the untreated baseline.
HEA coatings with smaller grains will exhibit less wear-track damage than the untreated baseline.
HEA coatings with coarser grains will exhibit diminished wear performance.
The proposed grain-size mechanism applies while grain sizes remain within the nanocrystalline-to-ultrafine regime.
Other wear mechanisms may dominate in coarse-grained coatings or under extreme-temperature or extreme-pressure wear conditions.
Direct evidence specifically linking grain-size modification to wear resistance in HEA coatings is limited.
Phase stability, coating adhesion, and residual stress may significantly influence HEA-coating wear behavior.
Failure of significantly refined samples to show a measurable wear-rate reduction relative to the as-deposited control would falsify the hypothesis.
